situation:
You are the human resources director at CALDER VALLEY UTILITIES, a water and power provider whose field crews handle every repair, restoration and new connection in the service area. The vice president of operations (judge) has asked you to meet before next year's staffing plan goes to the board.

CALDER VALLEY has served the region for over forty years, and its restoration times are the reason customers stayed when BRIGHTFIELD ENERGY entered the market and began taking accounts. Those times rest on senior crew leads who have worked the same lines for a decade and know where the trouble is before the customer finishes describing it. Field work is unpredictable, and the crews absorb that by working overtime.

The staffing analysis in front of you says overtime is the cheaper way to cover the same work. Adding twelve field technicians costs more per hour worked once benefits, vehicles and the year of training before a technician can lead a restoration are counted. The supervisors and the crews say the analysis is measuring the wrong thing. Overtime shows up in the pages as hours; the same hours show up in the trucks as fatigue, missed family time, and the senior leads talking about leaving.

Staying with the overtime model would hold payroll flat in the year BRIGHTFIELD is taking accounts, and the hours would keep falling on the same senior leads who say they are worn out. Hiring the twelve technicians would spread the load, and it would raise payroll while the company is losing customers, with the new hires a year away from leading a restoration.

The vice president of operations (judge) wants your recommendation on how CALDER VALLEY will cover field work next year, how you would weigh what the crews are telling you against what the analysis shows, and what it means for the customers who call. You will present to the vice president of operations (judge), who will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the vice president of operations (judge) at CALDER VALLEY UTILITIES. Business background is the same as the situation above. The staffing analysis says overtime is cheaper than adding twelve field technicians, the supervisors and crews say the analysis misses what the hours are doing to them, and BRIGHTFIELD ENERGY is taking accounts while the plan is decided.

You have asked the human resources director to recommend how the company will cover field work next year, how to weigh what the crews are saying against what the analysis shows, and what the decision means for the customers who call.

After the participant has presented, ask these questions:
judgeQuestions: Who ends up carrying the cost of what you are recommending?
Can we defend that to the crews who have been here longest?
